original_value: This study aimed to develop empirical pasture dry matter (DM) yield prediction models using an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-borne sensor at four flying altitudes. Three empirical models were developed using features generated from the multispectral sensor: Structure from Motion only (SfM), vegetation indices only (VI), and in combination (SfM+VI) within a machine learning modelling framework. Four flying altitudes were tested (25 m, 50 m, 75 m and 100 m) and based on independent model validation, combining features from SfM+VI outperformed the other models at all heights. However, the importance of SfM-based features changed with altitude, with limited importance at 25 m but at all higher altitudes SfM-based features were included in the top 10 features in a variable importance plot. Based on the independent validation results, data generated at 25 m flying altitude reported the best model performances with model accuracy of 328 kg DM/ha. In contrast, at 100 m flying altitude, the model reported an accuracy of 402 kg DM/ha which demonstrates the potential of scaling up this technology at farm scale. The spatial-temporal maps provide valuable information on pasture DM yield and DM accumulation of herbage mass over the time, supporting on-farm management decisions.

result.paraphrase: This study developed empirical models for predicting pasture dry matter (DM) yield using an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-mounted sensor at four flight altitudes. Within a machine learning framework, three models were built from multispectral-sensor-derived features: Structure from Motion only (SfM), vegetation indices only (VI), and a combined SfM+VI model. The tested altitudes were 25 m, 50 m, 75 m, and 100 m; independent validation showed that SfM+VI performed best at every height. The contribution of SfM-based features varied with altitude, being limited at 25 m but appearing among the top 10 variables in the importance plot at all higher altitudes. Independent validation also showed the strongest performance at 25 m, with an accuracy of 328 kg DM/ha. At 100 m, accuracy was 402 kg DM/ha, indicating the technology’s potential for scaling to farm level. The resulting spatiotemporal maps offer useful information on pasture DM yield and the accumulation of herbage mass over time, aiding on-farm management decisions.
